name: Window Is Already Closing
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Migration Clock Started Before You Noticed
lesson.summary: Post-quantum cryptography migration takes years, and because usable NIST standards already exist, the safe-to-wait window for most organizations closed earlier than their IT roadmaps assume.
lesson.body:
Cryptographers describe a threat called harvest-now-decrypt-later: an adversary records your encrypted traffic today and simply stores it, waiting for a future quantum computer capable of breaking the encryption. This reframes the urgent question. It is not "when will a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exist," it is "how long does my data need to stay secret, plus how long will migrating my systems take, compared to how long until that machine exists." Cryptographer Michele Mosca captured this as an inequality: if your data's required shelf life (X) plus your migration time (Y) exceeds the time remaining until a quantum threat arrives (Z), you are already exposed, even if the threat itself is still years away.

This connects directly to how large the quantum threat actually is. Building a machine that can run Shor's algorithm against RSA-2048 in a practical amount of time requires, by published error-corrected estimates, somewhere from roughly one million to over ten million noisy physical qubits, depending on assumptions about gate error rates and the error-correcting code used. Today's largest gate-based processors hold on the order of a few hundred to roughly a thousand-plus physical qubits, none of them meaningfully fault-tolerant at production scale. That gap looks like it buys a decade or more of runway, and for the pure physics question (Z), it probably does. But Z is only one variable in Mosca's inequality, and it says nothing about Y.

NIST finalized its first three post-quantum cryptography standards in August 2024: FIPS 203 (ML-KEM, for key exchange) and FIPS 204 and 205 (ML-DSA and SLH-DSA, for digital signatures). That means the "we're waiting for standards" excuse expired in 2024. Large organizations, banks, telecoms, government agencies, have historically taken the better part of a decade to migrate core cryptographic infrastructure once a replacement standard exists; the shift away from SHA-1 dragged on for years after it was known to be weak, largely due to vendor dependencies, legacy hardware, and third-party integration lag. There is no realistic reason to expect quantum-safe migration will move faster.

Put numbers to it: suppose your organization holds records that must stay confidential for X = 15 years, health or genomic data is a common example. Suppose a full, realistic migration of your cryptographic stack, given every vendor and integration dependency, takes Y = 8 years. X + Y = 23 years. Even a genuinely conservative, skeptical estimate that a cryptographically relevant quantum computer is Z = 20 to 25 years away means you are already inside, or very close to, the exposure window today. This is not a call to panic, it is arithmetic: waiting made sense only while there was no standard to migrate to. Now that one exists, every additional year of delay is unhedged risk with no offsetting benefit.

This sets up a tension the next chapter addresses directly. The same qubit-count skepticism that makes near-term codebreaking implausible is often misused to justify inaction on migration altogether. Window-closing is a logistics argument about how long organizations take to move, not a physics argument about how close quantum computers are. Holding both facts at once, quantum computers are not breaking your bank's encryption next year, and your organization should already be migrating, is exactly the discipline a skeptic's guide is meant to build.
